title: Back to the Future: Revisiting the Failed Futures of the Past (CS183 Class 15)
summary: Thiel argues the failed futures of the 1950s-60s (energy storage, weather, robotics, space) are fertile ground for startups: find where the past went wrong, learn the right lessons, and attack the problem from a radically different angle. He also covers why unique ideas are hard to fund, why enterprise sales must start small with good references, and how to disguise a sale.

principles.text: Revisit failed futures, but don't just copy them: learn from the past and deploy it in a new way.
principles.quote: The goal, then, is to tap into the past, learn all we can, and deploy that knowledge in some new, important way.

principles.text: Underexplored research lines may be worth revisiting if they were dropped for reasons other than merit.
principles.quote: Not everything that has gone underexplored deserves to be lost.

principles.text: Retrofuture: find where the past failed, learn the right lessons, and approach the old problem from a very different perspective.
principles.quote: The retrofuture idea is simply this: think about where the past failed, learn the right lessons, and make it work this time.

principles.text: Computer science is the exception: its visions of the future largely came true, while most other fields went off track.
principles.quote: But in most areas, things got seriously off track. The future didn't work.

principles.text: Long-term expert predictions (25-50 years) can be code for 'someone else will do it'; far horizons escape accountability.
principles.quote: But 25-50 years is really long-term; it's just beyond the horizon where people are no longer accountable.

principles.text: Bold, unfamiliar startups are hard to fund because investors can't evaluate what they don't know; but that also means few competitors.
principles.quote: The upside to doing something that you're unfamiliar with, like rockets, is that it's likely that no one else is familiar with it, either.
